title: Mooring Choice
primary_metric: net buoyant lift (buoyancy minus hull, sinker, and ballast weight) per dollar of material

options.A: The Spar Design -- a steel cylinder with a conical cutwater nose, moored to the shared pyramidal sinker
options.B: The Spherical Design -- a single steel sphere, moored to the same shared pyramidal sinker

deliverables.text: The Spar Design's total volume (cylinder + cone) and total exposed steel surface area (cylinder side + bottom cap + cone side), shown step by step.
The Spherical Design's total volume and total exposed steel surface area, with a written surface-area-per-unit-volume comparison to the Spar Design's D1 figures.
The shared pyramidal sinker's volume, total surface area, and submerged (apparent) weight.
A materials cost table: steel cost for each hull (from D1/D2's surface areas), the shared sinker's concrete cost (from D3), and the Spherical Design's stability-ballast mass and cost.
A net-buoyant-lift-per-dollar results table for both options and a written recommendation using that ratio.

appendices.title: Hull Dimensions, Steel, and the Real Buoys Behind Them
The Cost-and-Lift Comparison, Step by Step

balance.argument_a: The Spar Design's cylinder-and-cone shape gives it a naturally low center of gravity and stable ride with zero added ballast, unlike the Spherical Design, which needs stability ballast equal to 65% of its own hull steel weight (MA6) just to ride safely -- weight that buys the Spar nothing extra to carry. The Spar's steel cost ($5,381.06) is higher, but its flat cylindrical sides are simpler and cheaper for the shop to fabricate and to bolt instrument brackets onto than a curved spherical shell, a real, if unquantified in dollars, fabrication-labor advantage this case discloses but does not price.
balance.argument_b: A sphere encloses more volume per unit of steel surface area than a cylinder-and-cone shape of the same displacement: the Spherical Design's 16.62 m2 of exposed steel is about 29% less than the Spar's 23.37 m2 for essentially the same 6.4 m3 of buoyant volume, which directly lowers its steel cost ($3,826.05 vs. $5,381.06). Even after subtracting its 65%-of-hull-weight stability ballast (MA6), the Spherical Design still delivers more net buoyant lift per dollar of total material -- 0.826 kg/$ versus the Spar's 0.666 kg/$.
balance.margin_basis: RESOLVED at case-research. net buoyant lift = (hull volume x seawater density) - hull steel weight - sinker submerged weight - (Spherical Design only) stability ballast mass. Spar: displaced 6569.1 kg - steel 1834.8 kg - sinker submerged 1031.2 kg = 3703.0 kg net lift; total material cost = steel $5,381.06 + sinker $176.52 = $5,557.59; ratio = 0.6663 kg/$. Spherical: displaced 6529.9 kg - steel 1304.6 kg - sinker submerged 1031.2 kg - ballast 848.0 kg = 3346.1 kg net lift; total material cost = steel $3,826.05 + sinker $176.52 + ballast $50.00 = $4,052.58; ratio = 0.8257 kg/$. margin = |0.8257 - 0.6663| / 0.8257 = 19.3%. The Spherical Design (Option B) wins, but by 19.3% -- just inside SPEC Section 2's ~20% cap. The case's real teaching tension is that the sphere's steel-efficiency advantage from D1/D2 is real and large (about 29% less surface area for the same volume) but is substantially eaten into, not erased, by the stability ballast a sphere structurally requires and a spar does not -- a student who stops after D2's steel comparison will overstate the sphere's advantage.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Set equal to the Spar Design's own computed volume (radius 0.60 m cylinder, height 5.40 m, plus a 0.80 m cone of the same radius) -- a stated naval-architecture requirement sized to carry the sensor payload for both options fairly.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Scales both options' volume, displacement, and steel surface area together; does not by itself flip the dilemma.

modeling_assumptions.value_used: radius 0.60 m, cylinder height 5.40 m, cone height 0.80 m
modeling_assumptions.basis: Scaled to the real NDBC 6-meter NOMAD-class spar hull's general size [S6], without claiming a specific published engineering drawing.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Directly sets Option A's D1 volume/surface-area figures and so its steel cost and net lift.

modeling_assumptions.basis: A design choice sized to bring the Spherical Design's volume within about 1% of MA1's 6.41 m3 minimum, so the two options are compared at matched buoyant capacity.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Directly sets Option B's D2 volume/surface-area figures and so its steel cost and net lift.

modeling_assumptions.basis: A representative marine-grade hull-plate thickness for a data buoy of this size class; no public spec sheet was found for this exact buoy.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: HIGH -- scales both options' steel weight and cost together; swept in sensitivity_model.py.

modeling_assumptions.basis: A representative pyramidal mooring-sinker size for this buoy's displacement class, informed by NDBC's general description of pyramidal sinkers as a standard mooring-hardware shape [S7].
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Affects both options equally (shared sinker); does not by itself change the margin between A and B.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Spherical Design stability ballast, as a fraction of its own hull steel weight
modeling_assumptions.basis: The Spherical Design's shape lacks the Spar's natural low center of gravity; real spherical/discus mooring buoys carry internal ballast for this reason. No public figure exists for this exact hull.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: HIGH -- this is the case-defining assumption; see the Sensitivity note in case.md Appendix E and sensitivity_model.py's probe-5 sweep.

modeling_assumptions.basis: A small, fixed cost for scrap-steel or poured-concrete ballast material.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: LOW -- does not meaningfully move D5's ratio on its own.

sensitivity_note: margin_pct (19.3%) is directly and materially sensitive to MA6 (the Spherical Design's stability-ballast fraction) and, to a lesser degree, to MA4 (shared steel plate thickness, which scales both options' steel cost together). It is comparatively insensitive to MA5 and MA7, which affect both options equally or contribute a small fixed cost.

derived._note: Computed during case-write from Appendix A/B/C/D's stated figures; sensitivity_model.py re-derives these independently.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA6 (the Spherical Design's stability ballast, 65% of its own hull steel weight) is a stated design assumption -- no public spec exists for this exact hull's actual ballast requirement, and real spherical mooring buoys vary widely by intended sea state. Tier 2 probe 5's +/-50% sweep found this dial does not flip the winner but does widen the margin outside SPEC Section 2's 20% cap at -50% flex (margin rises to 39.6%, Spherical Design's advantage grows) -- a real, disclosed instability in the SIZE of the win, not its direction. A facilitator should be ready for a room that flexes this assumption to land on a much larger margin than the case's own 19.3%.

MA4 (shared steel hull plate thickness, 1 cm for both options) is a stated design assumption -- no public spec sheet exists for this exact buoy's hull plate gauge, and real marine hull plate thickness varies by class society rules and sea-state rating. Tier 2 probe 5's +/-50% sweep found this dial does not flip the winner (the Spherical Design stays ahead at every tested value) but does widen the margin outside the 20% cap at -50% flex (0.5 cm plate -> margin 28.3%) -- thinner plate benefits both options' steel cost, but the Spherical Design's already-smaller steel weight means the fixed-cost sinker and ballast terms make up a larger share of its total, changing the ratio faster than the Spar's. Disclosed rather than retuned, since MA4 is shared equally by both options by construction and the instability is in the margin's size, not the recommendation.
